x-e-m3-01.title: Fix a reason sentence that goes off topic in an opinion piece
x-e-m3-01.goal: Check whether each sentence in an opinion piece supports the claim, find the sentence that doesn't fit, and rewrite it as a reason sentence that fits the claim.
x-e-m3-01.material: In English class, a student wrote an opinion piece about 'Should school start later?' Each sentence is on its own line.
x-e-m3-01.thinking.0: Check how each sentence relates to the claim
x-e-m3-01.thinking.1: Find the reason that doesn't fit and fix it
x-e-m3-01.prereq.0: Easy connecting words that show a reason, like because and so
x-e-m3-01.prereq.1: English sentences that give an opinion with I think ...
x-e-m3-01.s.s1.prompt: Pick the one line in this opinion piece that does not support the claim.
x-e-m3-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, write one word for how it relates to the claim 'School should start later' (claim/reason/conclusion/other).
x-e-m3-01.s.s1.hint.1: For each line, ask: 'If this sentence is true, is it a reason to change the start time?'
x-e-m3-01.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is about lunch getting cold, so it does not connect to the school start time. Lines 2 and 3 support the claim with 'tired -> hard to focus'. Line 1 is the claim, and line 5 is the conclusion.
x-e-m3-01.s.s2.prompt: Delete the sentence you picked, and write in English one sentence that supports the same claim (School should start later).
x-e-m3-01.s.s2.hint.0: First, think of one way in Korean that a later start would change a student's morning.
x-e-m3-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does your new sentence say what is good about starting later, or what problem comes from starting early?
x-e-m3-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you add a new reason without repeating the same thing as lines 2 and 3 of the original piece?
x-e-m3-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is your sentence one complete English sentence?
x-e-m3-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: It gave a different reason, breakfast.
x-e-m3-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write that one thing in a single English sentence. You may start with "Also, ..." or start differently.
x-e-m3-01.s.s2.modelNote.2: It supports the same claim by describing a problem that arises when starting early.

x-e-m3-02.title: Write my own opinion piece: reasons and a response to the other side
x-e-m3-02.goal: Decide your own position and write a short opinion piece in English with reasons and a response to an opposing view.
x-e-m3-02.material: In English class you read the claim 'Students should have a short break between classes.' You want to persuade a friend who doesn't agree with this claim.
x-e-m3-02.thinking.0: Choose evidence that is useful for persuading
x-e-m3-02.thinking.1: Expect an opposing view and respond to it
x-e-m3-02.prereq.1: Easy connecting words like but and however
x-e-m3-02.s.s1.prompt: To persuade a friend who doesn't agree with this claim, which of the following pieces of evidence would be most useful?
x-e-m3-02.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine whether a friend who doesn't agree could hear this and ask, 'Really?'
x-e-m3-02.s.s2.hint.0: First decide whether you agree or disagree, and write the reason in one line in Korean.
x-e-m3-02.s.s2.hint.1: Write one line: 'What would someone who doesn't think so say?' Then continue with your answer to it, written in English.
x-e-m3-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is your position clearly one thing?
x-e-m3-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Does your reason explain 'why it is so'? (Did you avoid just repeating good/bad?)
x-e-m3-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you state the opposing view fairly before writing your response?
x-e-m3-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each option, mark who says it, how many people, and what is said to happen.
x-e-m3-02.s.s1.r.a: It connects an action (drinking water, resting) with a result (focus), so even someone who disagrees can check it.
x-e-m3-02.s.s1.r.b: "Everybody wants it" rests on popularity. It does not tell a friend who disagrees why it is good.
x-e-m3-02.s.s1.r.c: "Very good" is a strong expression, but it does not explain what is good and how.
x-e-m3-02.s.s1.r.d: It rests on who said it. It does not explain the content itself.
x-e-m3-02.s.s1.explain: To persuade a friend who disagrees, you need evidence that shows "what happens and so what result arises," more than the number of people or who is speaking. a connects an action and a result.
x-e-m3-02.s.s2.prompt: Write an opinion piece of 3 to 5 sentences in English about "Students should have a short break between classes." Include (1) your position, (2) a reason, and (3) one opposing view and your response to it. Either agreeing or disagreeing is fine.

x-e-m3-03.title: Sort out which of three reviews to use as evidence for a buying decision
x-e-m3-03.goal: Among three reviews, sort out which content can be evidence for a buying decision, and write advice that fits the situation in English.
x-e-m3-03.thinking.0: Tell facts from feelings in reviews
x-e-m3-03.thinking.1: Choose evidence that fits the situation and make a judgment
x-e-m3-03.prereq.0: Easy adjectives like good, cold, and hard
x-e-m3-03.prereq.1: Knowing what the stars in a review are
x-e-m3-03.s.s1.prompt: What is the best reason that Review B is more useful than Review A for making a buying decision?
x-e-m3-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether B's strength remains if you take away the star rating, the length, or the mention of problems, one at a time.
x-e-m3-03.s.s1.r.a: A low star rating is not more honest. A low rating can also be written without evidence.
x-e-m3-03.s.s1.r.b: Length alone doesn't tell you how much information there is. A long review can still have only feelings.
x-e-m3-03.s.s1.explain: B tells what happened, such as the times (8 a.m. to 2 p.m.), ice, the cap, and the paint, so you can compare it with your situation. A has only feelings. A low star rating or a long review doesn't guarantee the quality of evidence.
x-e-m3-03.s.s2.hint.0: Pick one piece of content in B that relates to soccer practice.
x-e-m3-03.s.s2.hint.1: Write one sentence each on whether it's okay to buy because of that content, and whether there is anything to worry about.
x-e-m3-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say which content in the reviews your judgment came from?
x-e-m3-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you avoid using a review with no information, like A or C, as your evidence?
x-e-m3-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Does the thing you still want to know connect to your judgment?
x-e-m3-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: It judged not to buy and filtered out the reviews without evidence.
x-e-m3-03.material:
Hana is going to buy a water bottle to use at soccer practice in the summer. She read three reviews of the "Mino Bottle" on an online shopping site.

Review A (5 stars): "Best bottle ever! I love it so much. Everyone should buy it!"

Review B (4 stars): "It kept my water cold from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. I put in ice, and some was still left. The cap is a little hard to open. After I dropped it twice, the paint came off."

Review C (1 star): "Very bad. The box came three days late, and the delivery man was rude."
x-e-m3-03.s.s1.hint.0: In each review, mark separately the concrete facts (time, condition of the item) and the expressions of feeling.
x-e-m3-03.s.s1.r.c: Mentioning a problem does not make the evidence good. What the problem is matters.
x-e-m3-03.s.s1.r.d: It says what happened, so a buyer can compare it with their own situation.
x-e-m3-03.s.s2.prompt: Hana needs a water bottle for soccer practice (all afternoon) in the summer. Based on the reviews, write two or three sentences of advice in English. Include whether to buy it or not, which review and what content you based it on, and one thing you still want to know.

x-e-m3-04.title: Change a restaurant choice as more reviews appear one by one
x-e-m3-04.goal: Read restaurant reviews step by step, revise your judgment, and write in English the conditions of a rating you can trust.
x-e-m3-04.material: A family is choosing a restaurant for lunch before a movie (starts at 3:00 p.m.). Lunch time is one hour starting at 12:30. The review information comes out one piece at a time.
x-e-m3-04.thinking.0: Revise your judgment with new information
x-e-m3-04.thinking.1: Generalize the conditions of a trustworthy rating
x-e-m3-04.prereq.0: The meanings of words like stars (rating) and review
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.prompt: Read the information one piece at a time, and judge whether to choose this restaurant for the family's lunch.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.hint.0: Find one word or number you see for the first time in this piece.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.hint.1: Check your earlier judgment against the new information, one thing at a time.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: With just this information, what is the most reasonable thought about choosing this restaurant?
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.0.after: Even if the rating is high, with only 3 reviews it is just 'looks good'. You need more information.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Seeing the new information, how should you view the 4.8 rating?
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Reviews with the same sentence, posted on the same day, don't look like independent opinions from different people. Trust in the rating has gone down.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: The family arrives at 12:30 and has to finish eating by 1:30. What should they do now?
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.2.after: With more reviews, there is now specific information, the waiting time. If you match it with your situation (1 hour), you get the judgment to make a reservation or pick another place.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.reflect: From your first judgment to the last, which new information changed it? Say one thing you came to trust more instead of the rating number.
x-e-m3-04.s.s2.prompt: Complete the sentence that starts with 'A restaurant rating is more reliable when ...' and write the conditions of a trustworthy rating in English.
x-e-m3-04.s.s2.hint.0: Think of the information that raised your trust the most in the reveal steps.
x-e-m3-04.s.s2.hint.1: Connect 'is more reliable when ...' using when.
x-e-m3-04.s.s2.placeholder: Example: A restaurant rating is more reliable when ...
x-e-m3-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does the condition you wrote connect to the information you saw in the reveal steps (number of reviews, the same sentence, waiting time)?
x-e-m3-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is your condition not just a repeat of 'the rating is high'?
x-e-m3-04.s.s2.modelNote.1: It gave being specific as a condition.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Few reviews does not mean it is bad. It just means we do not know yet.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: The star rating is high, but how many reviews there are matters. It is hard to be sure from the opinions of only 3 people.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: It looks at both that the star rating is good and that the number of reviews is small.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The number is the same, but whether the reviews that made the number are trustworthy has changed.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It combines the identical sentences with the clue of the opening day to become suspicious.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You cannot tell any relationship between opening-day reviews and the freshness of the food. The connection to the clue is weak.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: It checks the waiting-time information in the review against my own time limit.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: It saw only that the number went down. It did not take into account that these are opinions from more people.
x-e-m3-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The star rating is high, but it did not check the "40-minute wait" in the reviews against my time limit.

x-e-m3-05.title: Turn a message for a friend into an email to a teacher
x-e-m3-05.goal: Rewrite a short message to a friend as a formal email to a teacher, keeping all the necessary information.
x-e-m3-05.material:
Jiho can't go to Friday's band practice, so he sent his friend Mina this message.

"hey mina! cant come 2 band practice on fri. got a fever lol. tell ms. park pls. thx!!"

Now Jiho wants to send an email directly to Ms. Park.
x-e-m3-05.thinking.0: Tell apart what to change from what to keep depending on the reader
x-e-m3-05.prereq.0: The format of a letter that begins with Dear ...
x-e-m3-05.prereq.1: Spelling out contractions like can't and won't
x-e-m3-05.s.s1.prompt: Pick all the parts that need to change in the email to Ms. Park.
x-e-m3-05.s.s1.hint.0: Divide each part into 'tone' and 'information'. What information does the teacher need?
x-e-m3-05.s.s1.hint.1: Find expressions you used with your friend that the teacher might find strange.
x-e-m3-05.s.s1.r.a: It is a greeting you use with a friend. For a teacher, the form of address has to change.
x-e-m3-05.s.s1.r.b: The reason is information the teacher needs to know. The form can change, but the content must stay.
x-e-m3-05.s.s1.r.e: The date is information the teacher must know.
x-e-m3-05.s.s2.prompt: Be Jiho and write the body of an email to Ms. Park in English. Include a greeting, the reason you can't come and the day, an apology or request, a closing, and your name.
x-e-m3-05.s.s2.hint.0: Change each part you chose in s1 into wording you can use.
x-e-m3-05.s.s2.hint.1: Write one line at a time in this order: greeting -> reason and day -> apology or request -> closing.
x-e-m3-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you use a form of address and closing that suit a teacher?
x-e-m3-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you leave out neither the reason nor the day?
x-e-m3-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is the apology or request (such as asking about what was covered in practice) polite?
x-e-m3-05.s.s2.modelNote.1: It added a story about the doctor to make the reason more specific.
x-e-m3-05.s.s1.o.c: The request 'tell ms. park' (a request to pass a message to Mina on her behalf)
x-e-m3-05.s.s1.r.d: Shortened spellings do not suit formal writing. They should be changed to correct spellings.
x-e-m3-05.s.s1.r.f: Laughing expressions and many exclamation marks do not match the tone of formal writing.
x-e-m3-05.s.s1.explain: What needs to change is the way of speaking (greeting, shortened spellings, lol and exclamation marks) and the request ('tell ms. park'), which does not suit writing directly to a teacher. The reason (a cold) and the day (Friday) are information the teacher also needs to know, so they must stay.

x-e-m3-06.title: What more does the email need to get an answer?
x-e-m3-06.goal: Compare an event notice with a short email draft, sort out the information the person in charge must have to answer, and add it formally.
x-e-m3-06.thinking.0: Sort out the information needed to answer a question
x-e-m3-06.thinking.1: Add information the other person doesn't know
x-e-m3-06.prereq.0: The meanings of words like grade and eligible
x-e-m3-06.prereq.1: The basic format of a formal email
x-e-m3-06.s.s1.prompt: What more information should the email have for Mr. Kim to answer 'Can I join?' Pick all the things that are really needed.
x-e-m3-06.s.s1.hint.1: Check one by one whether the draft has information about those conditions.
x-e-m3-06.s.s1.r.a: There is no score in the notice's conditions. Information that isn't in the conditions is not needed to answer.
x-e-m3-06.s.s1.r.b: The notice states a grade condition (Grades 7-9), so the grade must be known.
x-e-m3-06.s.s1.r.c: He might be curious, but it has nothing to do with whether she can join.
x-e-m3-06.s.s1.r.d: The notice states the school's location (Hanbit-gu) as a condition, so it must be known.
x-e-m3-06.s.s1.r.e: The information it gives the reader is not connected to eligibility.
x-e-m3-06.s.s1.explain: The conditions in the notice are grade (Grades 7-9) and the school's location (Hanbit-gu). You need to know these two things to answer whether she can join. Scores, how she found out, and a favorite song are not in the conditions.
x-e-m3-06.s.s2.prompt: Write one or two English sentences to go after 'I want to join the speaking contest.' in the draft. Formally give the necessary information about Jieun so that Mr. Kim can answer.
x-e-m3-06.s.s2.hint.1: Try starting in the form I am a ... student at ...
x-e-m3-06.s.s2.placeholder: Example: I am a ... student at ...
x-e-m3-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is there enough information for the person in charge to judge whether she can join?
x-e-m3-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is your 'I' sentence polite and natural?
x-e-m3-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Do the question (Can I join?) and the information connect in one go?
x-e-m3-06.s.s2.modelNote.1: It asked more formally by using eligible.
x-e-m3-06.material:
Jieun saw a notice for her school's English speaking contest.

"Hanbit-gu English Speaking Contest. Open to students in Grades 7-9 who attend a school in Hanbit-gu. Register by October 30. Ask Mr. Kim if you have questions."

Jieun is in Grade 9 at Sunrise Middle School (a school in Hanbit-gu). The draft email Jieun wrote is as follows.

Subject: Question
Dear Mr. Kim,
I want to join the speaking contest. Can I join?
Sincerely,
Jieun
x-e-m3-06.s.s1.hint.0: Find the "Open to ..." sentence in the notice and write down separately what the eligibility is based on.
x-e-m3-06.s.s2.hint.0: Put the information you chose in s1 into one sentence.

x-e-m3-07.title: The hidden assumption in 'we sold 200 fewer lunches'
x-e-m3-07.goal: Find out what unstated assumption is needed for a claim to hold, and write in English another explanation that shakes that assumption.
x-e-m3-07.material:
This was posted on the bulletin board in front of the school cafeteria.

"This month, the cafeteria sold 200 fewer lunches than last month. So students did not like the new menu."
x-e-m3-07.thinking.0: Find the hidden assumption in a claim
x-e-m3-07.thinking.1: Suggest another explanation and information to check
x-e-m3-07.prereq.0: Sentences that give a reason using because and so
x-e-m3-07.prereq.1: Expressions that talk about possibility with maybe and could
x-e-m3-07.s.s1.prompt: For the conclusion 'The cafeteria sold 200 fewer lunches. So students did not like the new menu' to hold, what assumption is needed that was not stated?
x-e-m3-07.s.s1.hint.1: For each choice, ask whether it affects the conclusion, whether it is true or not.
x-e-m3-07.s.s1.r.a: What the menu contains is not directly connected to this conclusion. You need an assumption that explains why the number sold went down.
x-e-m3-07.s.s1.r.d: How much care went into the cooking has nothing to do with the conclusion. It doesn't deal with the cause of the difference in sales.
x-e-m3-07.s.s1.explain: To go from the fact that sales went down to 'it didn't suit their taste', other conditions (the number of students, the number of school days, etc.) have to be the same. If there were fewer students or fewer school days, sales would go down even with the same taste.
x-e-m3-07.s.s2.prompt: Think of another reason why sales went down and write it in English, and also write in one sentence what you would need to know to check whether that reason is right.
x-e-m3-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write down in Korean two things that may have changed between last month and this month (students, dates, events).
x-e-m3-07.s.s2.hint.1: Pick one of them and write it in English with Maybe ... because ...
x-e-m3-07.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Maybe sales were lower because ... We need to know ...
x-e-m3-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is the reason you gave an explanation other than 'they didn't like the new menu'?
x-e-m3-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Does the information to check connect to your reason? (e.g., compare the number of students)
x-e-m3-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is your reason a sentence that can be checked, not just a one-time guess?
x-e-m3-07.s.s2.modelNote.1: It gave a different reason, a field trip.
x-e-m3-07.s.s1.hint.0: First write in your own language what could be the cause of "fewer lunches were sold."
x-e-m3-07.s.s1.r.b: Only when the number of students and the number of school days are similar can you say the difference in sales is because of taste.
x-e-m3-07.s.s1.r.c: The popularity of the old menu is not used to compare the sales numbers of this month and last month.

x-e-m3-08.title: Evaluate an argument that speaks about everyone from one case
x-e-m3-08.goal: In an argument, find the line that draws a general conclusion from one case, say why that conclusion doesn't hold, and pick stronger evidence.
x-e-m3-08.material: In debate class, a student said this.
x-e-m3-08.thinking.0: Find the leap between evidence and conclusion
x-e-m3-08.prereq.0: Words for quantity like some, all, and one
x-e-m3-08.prereq.1: The form of an argument that goes I think ..., so ...
x-e-m3-08.s.s1.hint.0: In the lines that serve as evidence, count 'how many people' the story is about.
x-e-m3-08.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the range of people the conclusion talks about (how many) with the range of the evidence.
x-e-m3-08.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is where it skips. The evidence in line 2 is only the case of one older brother, but line 3 talks about 'all students'. Line 4 stands on the assumption that line 3 is right.
x-e-m3-08.s.s2.prompt: Write one or two sentences in English about why the conclusion in line 3 doesn't hold, mentioning a counterexample or what is missing.
x-e-m3-08.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the number of people in line 2 and line 3.
x-e-m3-08.s.s2.hint.1: Try starting with 'But ... might ...' in English.
x-e-m3-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say the difference between one case and all students?
x-e-m3-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you hint at what more evidence would make the conclusion convincing?
x-e-m3-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you imagine a specific counterexample (such as a student the video didn't help)?
x-e-m3-08.s.s2.modelNote.1: It mentioned the possibility of a counterexample and the evidence needed together.
x-e-m3-08.s.s3.prompt: What kind of evidence would be best to back up this conclusion more strongly?
x-e-m3-08.s.s3.hint.0: Check how many students each choice compares and what it compares.
x-e-m3-08.s.s3.hint.1: Think about whether 'liked it / it's popular' and 'scores went up' are the same kind of evidence.
x-e-m3-08.s.s3.r.d: It only added more from the same one person, so the number of cases didn't grow.
x-e-m3-08.s.s3.explain: The conclusion is about 'all students', so evidence that compares many students in two groups is best. Popularity, fame, and the same person's feelings don't show an effect.
x-e-m3-08.s.s1.prompt: In this argument, choose the one line where the evidence first fails to connect to the conclusion and skips ahead.
x-e-m3-08.s.s3.r.a: Being popular is a different matter from the effect of learning.
x-e-m3-08.s.s3.r.b: That a famous person made it also does not show an effect.
x-e-m3-08.s.s3.r.c: It splits many students into two groups and compares them, so it is closer to the range of the conclusion (all students).

x-e-m3-09.title: Rewrite the same notice for young students and for parents
x-e-m3-09.goal: Rewrite the same school notice with different vocabulary and information depending on the reader (lower elementary students, parents).
x-e-m3-09.material:
This is a notice for a school science fair (for teachers).

"Students must submit project proposals to their homeroom teacher by October 20. Late proposals will not be accepted. Projects will be displayed in the gym on November 3 from 1:00 to 3:00 p.m. Parents are welcome to attend."
x-e-m3-09.thinking.0: Choose the information the reader needs
x-e-m3-09.thinking.1: Match vocabulary and tone to the reader
x-e-m3-09.prereq.0: How to write the month and date in English (Nov. 3)
x-e-m3-09.s.s1.hint.0: In each choice, mark whether 'what to do, the date, and what happens if it's late' remain.
x-e-m3-09.s.s1.hint.1: Separately check whether any words a 10-year-old doesn't know remain.
x-e-m3-09.s.s1.r.c: Hard words remain, and the exact date is gone.
x-e-m3-09.s.s2.prompt: Now write a two- or three-sentence invitation to parents in English. Include the date, time, and place, and invite them politely.
x-e-m3-09.s.s2.hint.0: Mark everything parents need to know in the last two sentences of the notice.
x-e-m3-09.s.s2.hint.1: Start with Dear parents, and write the place and date in one sentence and the time in the next sentence.
x-e-m3-09.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Dear parents, you are invited to ...
x-e-m3-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Are the date, time, and place all correct?
x-e-m3-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you change 'Parents are welcome' into an inviting tone?
x-e-m3-09.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is the tone different from the notice for young students?
x-e-m3-09.s.s2.modelNote.1: It wrote the time as 1 p.m. to 3 p.m.
x-e-m3-09.s.s1.prompt: Which is the most fitting way to rewrite the first two sentences above so that a third-grade elementary student can read and follow them right away, without difficult words?
x-e-m3-09.s.s1.r.a: It kept the task, the date, and the consequence of being late, all in easy words.
x-e-m3-09.s.s1.r.b: It got shorter, but difficult words such as proposals, due, and accepted remain as they are.
x-e-m3-09.s.s1.r.d: It is easy and friendly, but the date and the consequence of being late are gone.
x-e-m3-09.s.s1.explain: When the reader is a young student, change the words to easy ones but keep what to do (give ideas), the date (October 20), and what happens if late. d is easy and friendly, but the date and the consequence of being late are gone, and b and c keep difficult words such as proposals, due, and submit.

x-e-m3-10.title: Find and fix wording in an ad that is true but misleading
x-e-m3-10.goal: Compare an ad's wording with the fine print, find expressions that are true but misleading, and rewrite them into wording that is honest and still appealing.
x-e-m3-10.thinking.1: Rewrite wording while keeping the facts
x-e-m3-10.prereq.0: The meanings of percent (%) and up to
x-e-m3-10.prereq.1: Easy adjectives like natural and real
x-e-m3-10.s.s1.prompt: Pick all the large-print phrases that could be misleading when compared with the small print.
x-e-m3-10.s.s1.hint.0: Match each large-print phrase to the small print by asking 'What exactly does it say?'
x-e-m3-10.s.s1.r.a: It is only the name of the drink. There is nothing in it to check for truth.
x-e-m3-10.s.s1.r.b: It isn't false, but it's easy to read as 'mostly fruit'. Compare it with the percentage in the small print.
x-e-m3-10.s.s1.r.d: The word 'up to' can be read as applying to all flavors. Compare it with the small print.
x-e-m3-10.s.s1.r.e: It is a fact in the small print. What you need to look at is how this print relates to the large-print phrases.
x-e-m3-10.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite this ad in English in two sentences or fewer so that it is honest but still makes people want to buy. Include exactly how much fruit juice there is and which flavor the discount applies to.
x-e-m3-10.s.s2.hint.0: For each phrase you chose in s1, pair it with one fact from the small print.
x-e-m3-10.s.s2.hint.1: Put that fact in as it is, and add positive words (sweet, fresh, this week).
x-e-m3-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Are the facts (5%, 50% off for the apple flavor only) not wrong in your rewritten wording?
x-e-m3-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Does it still have expressions that make people want to buy (taste, mood, price)?
x-e-m3-10.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid expressions that could be misread, like 'up to 50%'?
x-e-m3-10.s.s2.modelNote.1: It also said the discount on the other flavors.
x-e-m3-10.material:
This is a drink ad poster.

"Sweet Day Juice: Made with real fruit! 100% natural taste! Up to 50% off!"

Small print at the bottom of the poster: "Contains 5% fruit juice and added flavoring. 50% off is for the apple flavor only. Other flavors are 10% off."
x-e-m3-10.s.s1.hint.1: Write down what meaning an ordinary person would take from each phrase, then compare it with the small print.
x-e-m3-10.s.s1.r.c: It says "natural," but the small print says flavoring was added. Compare it with the small print.
x-e-m3-10.s.s1.explain: b says "made with real fruit" although it has only 5% fruit juice, c says "natural taste" but the small print says flavoring was added, and d's maximum discount applies only to the apple flavor. The name (a) and the small print (e) are facts themselves.
